previous.passage: Diesel and burnt coffee hung over the bus depot in Istanbul where Nikos and I had worked the night schedule for twenty-two years. We rarely talked; a nod at the start of each shift had always been enough. One evening I opened the dispatch drawer looking for a stapler and found a stack of my own letters to my mother, the ones I believed had been lost years ago, each stamped and returned. Nikos must have been keeping them safe since the depot's old mailroom closed. I said nothing. The next night he set a cup of tea at my elbow before I asked, and I left the drawer unlocked so he would know I had seen. Through the glass, a bus idled with its doors folded open, its headlights pale in the drizzle.

previous.passage: Who brings a ferry token to a wedding? Mele asked, watching Leilani turn the brass coin over her knuckles while the band tuned up. Leilani explained that her father gave one to every passenger who crossed the harbor in bad weather, a promise that the boat would come back for them. Mele had ridden that ferry for years; tonight she was only waiting for a message from the hospital where her brother lay in surgery. As the speeches began, Leilani pressed the token into Mele's palm. Mele held it through the toasts and the first dance, rubbing its worn edge whenever her phone stayed dark. When the screen finally lit, she did not read it at once. She closed her fingers around the brass first. Around them, guests clapped as the couple cut a cake shaped like a lighthouse.

previous.passage: Cut grass and wet chalk: that is what I remember of the field in Taipei the week after I missed the penalty in front of the whole stadium. Coach Yuxuan benched me without explanation. Each evening at dusk she handed me a flat ball from the equipment shed and a hand pump, and I knelt by the sideline pressing air into it while the others ran drills. At first I resented the task and pumped carelessly, so the ball sagged by morning. By the fourth night I was checking the valve, squeezing the seams, testing the bounce against my palm before I handed it back. Yuxuan never commented. On the last evening of the week she rolled the ball back to me and pointed at the penalty spot. The floodlights buzzed on, one bank at a time, and moths gathered in the glare.

previous.passage: Jeju Island had one bus stop on that stretch of the mountain road, a tin shelter where Minjun waited each afternoon after school. Eamon, who had fished with her father before her father left for Busan, sat down beside her and said, without greeting, that her aunt had heard. Minjun had told only one classmate that her father was not coming back. By the time Eamon reached the shelter, the story had already walked down the mountain without her, stopping at the market, the clinic, and finally her aunt's kitchen. previous.passage: Kyoto's eastern hills were slick with rain when the funicular stalled halfway up, and the attendant herded its two passengers onto a terrace café to wait. Takeshi chose the table farthest from Kenji, nodded once, and opened a newspaper he did not read. Kenji ordered tea and apologized to no one in particular for the weather. For twenty minutes their only exchange concerned the sugar bowl. Then the owner set down a dish of pickled plums, and Kenji, tasting one, murmured that his grandmother had made them saltier, with a shiso leaf folded inside each. Takeshi lowered his paper. His mother, he said, had done the same, and had refused to write the method down because a written recipe, she claimed, would stop listening to the cook. Kenji laughed, pulled his chair closer, and began to guess at proportions. By the time the funicular hummed back to life, they had filled a napkin with crossed-out numbers and were arguing, happily, about how long to dry the leaves.

Do you remember the rule you made in the Hamburg courtyard last summer, Grandfather Konrad? Beside the dry fountain, we were to speak only German, even if I needed ten minutes to ask for a glass of water. I complained, and you pretended not to understand me until I found the verbs. Yesterday I sat on that stone rim again and, without thinking, asked a neighbor's child for directions in German. She answered in German, and I understood every word. I had planned to write that the rule could end now that I am nearly fluent. Instead I find I would rather keep it, because beside that fountain your language has started to feel like mine too. The fountain itself is still dry, but someone has planted red geraniums in its basin.
With love, Mira
